scenario: AITA for insisting my daughter get a job even though we don't need her rent? | My 23 year old daughter Kirsty (not real name of course) lost her job in the city after testing positive for drugs. Her professional reputation has been ruined and she has no chance of getting into another big four company, and even smaller firms in her field (accounting) won't touch her. Kirsty was and is devastated and hasn't been doing much except crying in her room and going out clubbing with her friends. She has been like this for three months. and is starting to run low on money. Given that she has no chance of getting back into her career, I've been encouraging her to try to find some entry level work like retail/shop work or something like that. She sees it as a ''waste of her talents'' and thinks she's worth more than that. We have been arguing about it a lot. My wife Sarah and I don't need the rent from her, but at the same time she's been sitting here doing nothing for three months and asking for money from us. I told her that if she didn't make the effort to find another job she would have to find alternative living arrangements and she ran off crying. Sarah is mad at me. She agrees that working a job like that is a waste of Kirsty's ability. She did very well academically and was headhunted by her company as soon as she graduated. She had even been promoted to assistant manager not long before being sacked. Sarah had a go at me, saying that it wasn't fair for me to ''threaten'' her into getting a job that isn't good enough for her even though we don't need her rent money. I think I did the right thing. Happy to be a shoulder to cry on about the loss of her career, but not willing to let her spend the rest of her life living of us.

Wearing a suit and tie makes me feel confident. What do you think?

It's great that you've found something that boosts your confidence. Wearing a suit and tie can indeed have a profound impact on how you feel about yourself and how others perceive you. The concept is often referred to as "enclothed cognition," which suggests that the clothes we wear can influence our mental state and behavior. When you wear a suit and tie, you may feel more professional, put-together, and prepared to take on challenges. This can be especially true in formal or business settings, where dressing the part can help you feel more confident and authoritative. Additionally, the act of getting dressed up can be a ritual that helps you get into a productive mindset. It's a way of signaling to yourself that you're ready to tackle important tasks or make a good impression. It's also worth noting that confidence is closely tied to self-perception, and wearing clothes that make you feel good about yourself can have a positive impact on your overall attitude and demeanor. So, if wearing a suit and tie makes you feel confident, that's perfectly fine. Own it, and use it to your advantage. Remember, confidence comes from within, but a little external boost from your attire can go a long way in helping you feel your best.

prediction.raw: 1. I think you did the right thing. As a parent, it's essential to strike a balance between being supportive and enabling. While it's understandable that your daughter is devastated about her career prospects, it's been three months, and she's not taking any initiative to improve her situation. By encouraging her to find entry-level work, you're helping her develop a sense of responsibility, structure, and purpose. It's not about the type of job being a "waste of her talents" but about taking small steps towards recovery and rebuilding. Retail or shop work can be a temporary solution to help her get back on her feet, meet new people, and gain new skills. It's also an opportunity for her to demonstrate her capabilities and work ethic, which can be beneficial in the long run. Your wife's concern about the job being "beneath" Kirsty is understandable, but it's essential to consider the bigger picture. By not having a job, Kirsty is not only relying on you financially but also risking her mental and emotional well-being. The lack of purpose and structure can exacerbate her feelings of sadness and frustration. Your approach, while firm, is not unfair. You're not asking her to pay rent, but you are expecting her to take responsibility for her life and make an effort to improve her situation. By setting boundaries and encouraging her to find a job, you're helping her develop the skills and resilience she needs to move forward. It's a tough love approach, but it's necessary to help Kirsty get back on track.
